subject: zoology_2
question_text: Distinguish between homologous and analogous organs.

verification.note: Sourced from 'My Baby Bullet-Q — Senior Inter Zoology' (Star-Q Pass Track Series, Sri Publishers, 2022), book p.40, SAQ 36. The printed exam years are the book's claim, reproduced here as appearances. Zoology-II holds only ONE source book in the corpus, so the two-book union check is structurally impossible for this card; 'not checked' does NOT mean 'checked and clean'. The mark split is our reading of the question and is a claim until a Telangana IPE teacher confirms it. Revised 2026-09-05 after the examiner audit: the insider note no longer claims this is the most repeated four-mark question, and the notes no longer ask for two columns, which the printed answer does not use.

steps.label: Homologous organs
steps.why: Same origin means the organs were inherited from a shared ancestor, whatever job they later took on.
common_mistakes: Defining homologous organs by function. They are defined by structure and origin.
steps.memory_tip: Homologous: same origin, different job — divergent.
steps.margin_note: Write the homologous block first, then the analogous block, using the same three points in the same order: definition, kind of evolution, example.
lines: Organs that have a similar structure and
origin but not necessarily the same

steps.label: Their examples
steps.why: The bones inside are arranged the same way in all of them, which is what shows the shared ancestor even though the uses differ.
common_mistakes: Giving the wings of an insect as an example. Only vertebrate forelimbs are homologous here.
Leaving out that the bone arrangement is the same.
steps.memory_tip: Flipper, wing, hand — one bone plan, four different jobs.
steps.margin_note: Name three or four examples in one line.
lines: the flipper of a whale, the wing of a bird,
the hand of man and the wing of a bat.
All these organs have the same arrangement
of bones, but their functions vary to suit

steps.label: Analogous organs
steps.why: When two unrelated animals face the same problem they often arrive at the same solution, and that is convergent evolution.
common_mistakes: Swapping divergent and convergent. Analogous organs suggest convergent evolution.
Defining analogous organs by origin. They are defined by function.
steps.memory_tip: Analogous: different origin, same job — convergent.
steps.margin_note: Use the same wording pattern as the homologous block: definition first, then the kind of evolution it suggests.
lines: Organs that have a different origin but
the same function are analogous organs.

steps.label: Their examples
steps.why: A butterfly's wing and a bird's wing are built from completely different tissues, yet both do the same job.
common_mistakes: Naming the bat and the bird together. Those are homologous.
steps.memory_tip: Butterfly wing and bird wing: same job, no shared origin.
steps.margin_note: One example and the closing rule.

insider_note: Asked eight times in the printed papers, more than any other four-mark question in this paper. Write the homologous block first, then the analogous block, and name divergent evolution and convergent evolution: those two words carry the two definitions.
